tagline.text: Ilocano heritage festival held in Vigan for the province's founding anniversary

location.label: Location
location.text: Vigan City, Ilocos Sur (around the provincial capitol, St. Paul Cathedral and Calle Crisologo)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Late January–early February (around the February 2 provincial anniversary)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱2,000–4,000 (per day, lodging, food and transport)

children.text: The Kannawidan Ylocos Festival is Ilocos Sur's signature festival, held every year from late January to early February around Vigan to commemorate the split of Ilocos into north and south on February 2, 1818. It brings traditional games, cultural shows, street dancing, period-costume dinners and an agricultural fair.

Kannawidan Ylocos is a cultural festival held every year by the province of Ilocos Sur. The name "Kannawidan" is said to come from the Ilocano word "tawid," meaning tradition or heritage. The festival is timed to February 2, 1818, when a Spanish royal decree divided the old province of Ilocos into Ilocos Norte and Ilocos Sur, and it grew out of the provincial founding-anniversary celebration.

The festival is said to have first been held in 2008 under Governor Deogracias Victor Savellano. Its aims are to promote and preserve local culture, traditions, customs and heritage, to showcase local products and craftsmanship, and to boost tourism. The main events take place in the capital, Vigan City, but some events, such as beach competitions and motor shows, spread to nearby towns and cities, so the whole festival runs well over a week.

The dates shift a little every year; sources describe the period as running from the last few days of January to the first week of February, or from the last week of January to the second week of February. For example, the 10th festival in 2017 ran from January 27 to February 13. I could not find an official 2026 announcement at the time of writing, so check the Ilocos Sur provincial government and Vigan City announcements before you go. The 2017 schedule gives a sense of the structure. There were events spread across the province, such as water and beach contests at Cabugao Beach Resort, a table tennis tournament in Santo Domingo, education days, technology and livelihood training, a rodeo, a game fowl expo and a motor show in Santa Catalina, while Vigan hosted the Saniata pageant preliminaries and talent show, a band competition, a cooking contest and longganisa-eating contest, a fashion show, a comedy night and a zarzuela. These were past editions, so do not assume the same lineup this year.

The best part of this festival is that it takes place on the cobbled streets of Vigan, a UNESCO World Heritage city. By day you can watch street dancing, traditional games and the fair, and in the evening enjoy a period-costume dinner in a historic building or a night show. The festival adds to Vigan's everyday sightseeing, so lodging fills earlier and the streets get more crowded than usual. Another thing to know is that the festival is not only for tourists. Many events are community competitions and award ceremonies (the Fr. Jose Burgos Awards, school and group awards, Department of Trade and Industry product awards and so on), so it is a meaningful way to see local pride up close. Go expecting a local celebration rather than a huge production, and you will enjoy it more.

Toward the end of the festival, street dancing and regional dance competitions take over the streets of Vigan. Colorful traditional costumes and drumming make downtown Vigan at its liveliest. In 2017 it was held on February 7, but the date changes every year.

These are dinners where prominent families and personalities wear traditional Filipino attire at historic venues. Places such as Burgos House, Calle Crisologo and the Ilocos Sur Museum have been mentioned as venues, and the date changes each year. Attendance may be by invitation or reservation, so check in advance.

blocks.title: Procession of the province's patron saints

children.text: In the opening days, Mass was held at St. Paul Cathedral, followed by a procession of the patron saints of the province's 34 towns and cities. It is an event that conveys the deep Catholic faith of Ilocos.

blocks.title: Traditional games and Ilocano culture contests

children.text: Contests on Ilocano culture are held, including traditional games, indigenous and folk dances, folk songs, poetry writing and a provincial history quiz. The province runs the festival with local residents at the center, so you can see the local atmosphere up close.

An agricultural and trade fair called Partuat ken Patanor runs alongside, where you can see Ilocos farm products, crafts and food in one place. It is also a chance to taste local food such as Vigan longganisa.

Drone light shows, dancing fountain shows, fireworks, comedy nights and pet shows are mentioned in different years, with the lineup changing a little from year to year. With so much to do at night, it pairs well with daytime sightseeing.
In 2017, a Kannawidan ritual with indigenous tribes was held in Barangay Tamag, Vigan, alongside bonsai, craft and heritage exhibits. The program differs every year, so check this year's schedule.

Even after the festival ends, Vigan can fill a day with its Spanish colonial streets, kalesa carriages, pottery workshops and longganisa. Combining the festival with regular sightseeing for at least a 2-day, 1-night stay makes the trip more satisfying.

items.title: 1 night 2 days festival course
items.subtitle: Overnight bus from Manila, two days in Vigan

children.text: Arrive in Vigan by overnight bus from Manila, leave your bags at your lodging and have Vigan longganisa for breakfast. Book your lodging in advance during the festival.
Walk around Plaza Salcedo and St. Paul Cathedral and check the places and times of that day's events.
Have lunch of Ilocano dishes (bagnet, pinakbet and more) and browse local products at the fair.
Tour the cobbled district by kalesa carriage. Traffic is slow during events, so leave extra time.
Watch the night shows in the evening, and if there is a dinner event, check whether you need to reserve.
On the second day, see a daytime event such as street dancing and head back to Manila in the afternoon. Return buses are crowded on the last day of the festival, so buy your ticket in advance.

items.subtitle: Combine the festival with northern highlights

children.text: See the daytime festival events in Vigan.

Vigan's historic district can be covered on foot, and kalesa carriages and tricycles are also available. On some days vehicles are restricted in the event area.
Venues in nearby towns and cities can be reached by bus or tricycle. Check how to get to each venue locally.

The festival is held in late January to early February in the middle of the dry season, so the weather is clear and cool. Daytime is warm but not as hot as midsummer, which is good for watching outdoor events.
The program and period change every year. The basic plan is to go around February 2, but decide the exact schedule from the provincial government's announcement.

Typical lodging is boutique hotels and guesthouses in restored Spanish colonial mansions in Vigan's historic district. During the festival they fill quickly, so it is safest to book at least several weeks ahead. If Vigan has no rooms, you can stay in Laoag or a nearby city and travel by bus.

Typical foods are Vigan longganisa (a strongly spiced sausage) and Ilocano dishes such as bagnet, pinakbet and empanada. Local snacks are also available at the fair. The event area is crowded at lunch and dinner, so going at off-peak times is more comfortable. Street stalls around the venues sell simple snacks, and souvenirs such as Ilocos vinegar, salt and woven goods can be found at the fair or in shops in town. Restaurants are crowded at lunchtime, so allow for queues, and check menu prices before ordering if prices are not posted.
The festival dates and program change every year, so check the Ilocos Sur provincial government and Vigan City announcements before you leave.
Book lodging and round-trip Manila buses at least several weeks ahead. Around February 2 and on street dancing day they fill up.
Street dancing often starts in the morning and continues into the afternoon. Go early to get a spot with shade and a good view.
Period dinners may be by invitation or advance reservation, so ask first if you want to attend.
Part of the event area is closed to vehicles. Check beforehand whether it is walkable from your hotel.
Guard against loss in crowds by wearing your bag in front and splitting your cash.
Watch religious events (Mass, processions of saints) quietly and photograph respectfully.
Bring a hat and water for hot days and a light jacket for evenings.
The official schedule is often posted only a week or two before the event. Book flights and buses with terms that let you adjust dates slightly.
The festival schedule changes every year, and some programs may change because of weather or administrative reasons. Check the official announcements once more right before you leave.
I could not confirm the official 2026 program. The events listed are based on past editions and general descriptions.
During the event, lodging prices rise and traffic gets heavy. Leave extra travel time.
Beware of pickpockets in crowded places.
Some events (drag racing, motor shows and so on) involve noise and safety restrictions. Follow the staff's instructions.
Dress and behave respectfully at religious events.
Vigan
, the festival's central city, is a UNESCO World Heritage Spanish colonial town famous for its kalesa carriages and longganisa.
Santa Maria Church
, about
40 km
south of Vigan, is a UNESCO World Heritage church that pairs well with a Vigan itinerary.
Laoag
is the main city of Ilocos Norte and the transport gateway thanks to its airport.
Paoay Church
is a World Heritage church in Ilocos Norte and a good addition to a circuit after the festival.
